target_customer: Private pilots with empty seats and passengers willing to split fuel and flight costs
problem: Small planes fly with empty seats; Flytenow was an online bulletin board where pilots posted flights and passengers joined to share expenses.
business_model: Online bulletin board for pilot expense sharing; revenue model not stated in sources read

founders.name: Matt Voska
founders.background_notes: YC bio: ops heavy technical cofounder, dual rated pilot.

founders.name: Alan Guichard
founders.background_notes: No bio on the YC page.

founders.name: Andrew Mass
founders.background_notes: No bio on the YC page.

founders.name: Aakash Patel
founders.background_notes: Named as a founder by VentureBeat on 2014-08-08 but not on the YC page; the founders were students in Boston.

exit.reason: After the D.C. Circuit upheld the FAA position on December 18, 2015, the company announced it would shut down.

competitors.name: AirPooler
competitors.what: Platform matching private pilots with passengers to share flight costs

technical_complexity.rationale: A bulletin board web product; the hard part was regulatory, not technical.

defensibility.rationale: AirPooler and others ran the same model and the legal position was untested; no data moat was described.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: The FAA ruled in August 2014 that online expense sharing was holding out as a common carrier requiring a Part 119 certificate; the court agreed on December 18, 2015.

market_need_then: Ride sharing was booming (Zimride, Lyft analogies in VentureBeat) and pilots wanted to split costs, but the FAA position on compensation was unclear at founding.

branding.domain_note: Used flytenow.com (exact name .com); it redirects to the company blog.

identity.logo: A plain F icon in directory listings (not verified from the company)
identity.voice_and_tone: Advocacy voice on the blog after the ruling; it rejected the Uber for planes label and said pilots only split fuel costs.

branding.community_and_virality: National press during the FAA fight (NBC, TechCrunch, Vice, CBS); the blog later pushed legislation, the Aviation Empowerment Act.

brand_strength.rationale: Large press from the legal case but the brand was tied to the dispute; sources show no merch or community outside it.

pivots.from: Pilots posting flights with expense sharing
pivots.to: Platform with expense sharing removed after the FAA ruling
pivots.why: FAA said online expense sharing amounted to holding out as a common carrier

outcome_analysis: Flytenow joined YC in summer 2014 and was hit by an FAA ruling in August that its model required commercial certification. It removed expense sharing, sued in January 2015, lost at the D.C. Circuit on December 18, 2015 and shut down, while the Supreme Court declined review in January 2017. Regulation, not demand or competition, is the stated cause.
notes: All three rounds rest on a single outlet (VentureBeat, 2014-08-08); the 120K YC amount is also given by Persana (aggregator, dated 2014-09-19) and Village.ai gives a 145K total that matches the sum, while CB Insights shows only 20K and is treated as incomplete. VentureBeat says the founders were students in Boston and does not name schools; education left empty. Wikipedia says the Supreme Court declined to hear the case on January 9, 2017 (seen in a search summary). AOPA in August 2014 named other flight sharing startups (ShareMySky, AiirShare, Pro Rata Share, Wingman); not added because the dates and traction were not verified.
